h: A student's discovery and a giant chamber
p: White Scar Cave was discovered in 1923 by a Cambridge student, Christopher Long, who squeezed his way in with candles and nerves of steel. It's quite something to think about as you stroll along the lit walkways that make the journey so much easier today. The guides love telling his story, and it gives the whole tour a sense of adventure.

The undoubted highlight is the Battlefield Cavern, a huge chamber that opens up towards the end of the route. After the narrower passages, stepping into that space is a proper jaw-drop moment, with formations hanging from the roof and a feeling of real scale. Don't rush it; take a minute to look around and soak it up.

A few practical tips: there are some low sections where you'll need to duck, so taller visitors should keep their wits about them, and the route involves steps and slopes, so it's not suitable for everyone with limited mobility. Check the cave's own information if that's a concern for your group.
Give yourselves time before or after for the café and the views from the hillside, which look out over some of the finest limestone country in the Dales.

For bigger adventures nearby, the Ribblehead Viaduct is a short drive up the valley and makes for a stunning photo stop, especially if a train happens to cross. Whernside and Ingleborough, two of the Yorkshire Three Peaks, rise on either side, so walkers have plenty to tackle. Ingleborough Cave at Clapham is also close by if you fancy seeing a second, very different show cave on the same trip.
